question: Roger Bannister ran the first sub-four-minute mile, at Iffley Road in Oxford.
explainer: Three minutes 59.4 seconds — then, one imagines, a very nice sit down.

question: The Sex Pistols released "God Save the Queen" during the Silver Jubilee.
explainer: No future — and definitely no royal warrant.

question: Doctor Who was broadcast on the BBC for the very first time.
explainer: The day after JFK was shot, which rather stole its thunder.

question: The National Health Service was founded.
explainer: Aneurin Bevan's big idea. We've been happily arguing about it ever since.

question: Tim Berners-Lee wrote his proposal for what became the World Wide Web, at CERN.
explainer: "Vague but exciting," wrote his boss on the cover. Fair.

question: The original Mini went on sale, designed by Alec Issigonis.
explainer: Four wheels, next to no boot, and endless charm.

question: Ian Botham dragged England to an improbable Ashes win at Headingley.
explainer: Following on, 500-1 against, and Beefy said hold my beer.

question: Live Aid filled Wembley Stadium and Philadelphia for famine relief.
explainer: Queen stole the show in twenty minutes flat.

question: Coronation Street aired its very first episode.
explainer: Still going strong. Ena Sharples would be astonished.

question: The Great Fire of London raged through the City for four days.
explainer: Started in a Pudding Lane bakery. Cheers, Thomas Farriner.

question: Alexander Fleming noticed a stray mould had killed his bacteria — penicillin.
explainer: The tidiest accident in medical history began with a very untidy lab.

question: The Great Bell of Westminster — Big Ben — rang out for the first time.
explainer: The bell, not the tower. That one's worth points down the pub.

question: Red Rum won the first of his three Grand Nationals.
explainer: Southport's finest. Ran down Crisp on the run-in.

question: Queen released "Bohemian Rhapsody" as a single.
explainer: Six minutes long. The record company nearly fainted.

question: The first Harry Potter film, "Philosopher's Stone", reached British cinemas.
explainer: Platform nine and three-quarters, and a nation's childhood.

question: Argentina invaded the Falklands and Britain sent a task force.
explainer: Eight thousand miles away, and seventy-four days long.

question: Sir Clive Sinclair's ZX Spectrum home computer went on sale.
explainer: 48K of memory and a loading screech you can still hear now.

question: Charles, Prince of Wales, married Lady Diana Spencer at St Paul's.
explainer: 750 million watched. "The stuff of which fairy tales are made."

question: Diego Maradona knocked England out of the World Cup with the "Hand of God".
explainer: The hand of God, apparently. The linesman's shrug agreed.

question: The Spice Girls released their debut single "Wannabe".
explainer: Girl power arrived, and told you what it really, really wanted.

question: "Monty Python's Flying Circus" first appeared on the BBC.
explainer: And now for something completely different. Literally.

question: Guy Fawkes and the Gunpowder Plot tried to blow up Parliament.
explainer: 36 barrels of gunpowder, one cellar, and one very bad night.

question: Louise Brown, the world's first IVF baby, was born in Oldham.
explainer: The "test-tube baby" who was, of course, born perfectly normally.

question: Blackpool Tower opened to the public.
explainer: Inspired by Paris. The Eiffel Tower, but with more rock and donkeys.

question: London hosted the Summer Olympic Games.
explainer: Jess, Mo and Greg all struck gold inside 44 magical minutes.

question: David Bowie released "The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars".
explainer: Bowie became an alien rock god, and pop never recovered.

question: "EastEnders" broadcast its first episode from Albert Square.
explainer: Dirty Den, Angie, and forty years of gloom to come.

question: The United Kingdom joined the European Economic Community.
explainer: In on New Year's Day. Leaving took rather longer.

question: Concorde made its maiden flight.
explainer: Mach 2, a droopy nose, and dinner in New York before you left.

question: Diana, Princess of Wales, died in a car crash in Paris.
explainer: A sea of flowers gathered at the palace gates for weeks.

question: Manchester United won the League, FA Cup and Champions League in one season.
explainer: Two goals in stoppage time in Barcelona. "Football, bloody hell."

question: Oasis released their debut album "Definitely Maybe".
explainer: The fastest-selling debut album in British history, at the time.

question: "Fawlty Towers" first checked in on BBC Two.
explainer: Twelve episodes. Not one of them wasted.

question: King John sealed Magna Carta in a meadow beside the Thames.
explainer: The barons had had quite enough, thank you very much.

question: Apollo 11 landed and Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon.
explainer: Half a billion people watched a man bounce about on the telly.

question: Cadbury launched its Dairy Milk chocolate bar.
explainer: A glass and a half of full-cream milk, and a nation hooked.

question: Andy Murray became the first British man in 77 years to win Wimbledon.
explainer: Fred Perry could finally rest. A whole nation exhaled.

question: Rick Astley's "Never Gonna Give You Up" hit UK number one.
explainer: Decades early for its true calling: the internet's oldest prank.

question: "The Great British Bake Off" first aired, on BBC Two.
explainer: Cakes, a tent, and the gentlest reality TV ever made.

question: Tony Blair led Labour to a landslide and became Prime Minister.
explainer: D:Ream were scientifically wrong, but it made a lovely anthem.

question: The Penny Black, the world's first adhesive postage stamp, was issued.
explainer: Rowland Hill's idea. Lick, stick, and away it went.

question: Antony Gormley's "Angel of the North" was installed near Gateshead.
explainer: 175 tonnes of rusty steel, with wings wider than a jumbo jet.

question: England won the Rugby World Cup with a last-minute drop goal.
explainer: Jonny Wilkinson's wrong foot did it, deep in extra time, in Sydney.

question: Wham! released "Last Christmas".
explainer: Kept off number one at the time. Utterly immortal since.

question: "Blue Peter" was first broadcast on the BBC.
explainer: Sticky-back plastic and good behaviour for over sixty years.

question: Decimal Day arrived and Britain swapped shillings for new pence.
explainer: Farewell half-crowns, farthings and thruppenny bits.

question: Crick and Watson, using Franklin's data in Cambridge, revealed DNA's structure.
explainer: "We've found the secret of life," announced, naturally, in the pub.

question: The Beano comic published its very first issue.
explainer: Gnasher, Dennis, and eighty-odd years of catapults since.

question: Torvill and Dean skated Boléro to a perfect set of sixes at the Winter Olympics.
explainer: Nottingham's own. Sarajevo, and every judge quietly swooning.

question: Amy Winehouse released her album "Back to Black".
explainer: A beehive, five Grammys, and a voice from another era.

question: The Eden Project opened its giant biomes in a Cornish clay pit.
explainer: The world's biggest greenhouses, dropped into a hole near St Austell.

question: The year-long miners' strike began under Arthur Scargill.
explainer: Pit villages, picket lines and a bruising year for Britain.

question: Concorde made its final commercial passenger flight.
explainer: The future of flight retired gracefully into a row of museums.

question: Prince Harry married Meghan Markle at Windsor Castle.
explainer: A gospel choir, a fiery sermon, and telly ratings galore.

question: Leicester City won the Premier League against 5,000-1 odds.
explainer: Vardy, Mahrez, and the greatest fluke in sporting history.

question: Blur and Oasis went head-to-head for number one in the "Battle of Britpop".
explainer: "Country House" won the week. Oasis had the last laugh, mind.

question: The world's first underground railway opened in London.
explainer: Steam trains. Underground. The Victorians feared absolutely nothing.

question: The UK voted to leave the European Union in a referendum.
explainer: 52 to 48. We've all been terribly relaxed about it since.

question: The first Raspberry Pi, a tiny British computer, went on sale.
explainer: A £25 computer the size of a credit card. It sold out in hours.

question: The Routemaster double-decker bus entered service in London.
explainer: That open rear platform you could leap onto. Health and safety wept.

question: Lewis Hamilton won his first Formula One World Championship.
explainer: On the last corner of the last lap of the last race. Casual.

question: Adele released her album "21".
explainer: Rolling in the deep, and at the top of the charts for the better part of a year.

question: "Teletubbies" first waddled onto children's television.
explainer: Baffling to adults, adored by toddlers, feared by no one.

question: Anti-poll-tax protests erupted into a riot in Trafalgar Square.
explainer: The charge that helped finish off Mrs Thatcher.

question: Halley's Comet last swung past Earth (next due in 2061).
explainer: Once in a lifetime — unless you're really planning ahead.

question: The Shard, then western Europe's tallest building, was officially opened.
explainer: 1,016 feet of glass splinter over London Bridge.

question: Gazza's tears at the World Cup semi-final made grown men weep too.
explainer: Italia '90, a yellow card, and a nation falling for football again.

question: Band Aid recorded "Do They Know It's Christmas?" for famine relief.
explainer: Feed the world — and every pop star Bob Geldof could get on the phone.

question: The first Notting Hill Carnival took to the streets of west London.
explainer: From a small local do to Europe's biggest street party.

question: The Great Exhibition opened in Hyde Park's vast Crystal Palace.
explainer: Prince Albert's giant glasshouse showed off the entire world.

question: Stephenson's Rocket won the Rainhill Trials for steam locomotives.
explainer: Not the first engine, but the shape of every one that followed.

question: London introduced its congestion charge for driving into the centre.
explainer: Ken Livingstone's fiver to drive into town. Now rather more than a fiver.

question: Bradley Wiggins became the first Briton to win the Tour de France.
explainer: Sideburns, a mod, and yellow in Paris — then Olympic gold days later.

question: Pulp released "Common People".
explainer: Jarvis, art school, and the anthem of a decade.

question: "Goldfinger", the third James Bond film, arrived in cinemas.
explainer: Shirley Bassey belting, and one very unlucky woman painted gold.

question: Britain celebrated Victory in Europe Day as the war in Europe ended.
explainer: Bunting, street parties, and the King and Churchill on the balcony.

question: The Sinclair C5 battery tricycle went on sale — and promptly flopped.
explainer: Clive's electric future. 15mph, and terrifying next to a lorry.

question: Marmite was first produced, in Burton-on-Trent.
explainer: Yeast extract from brewers' leftovers. Divisive from day one.

question: England's women won the European Championship at Wembley.
explainer: Chloe Kelly's shirt-twirling winner, in front of a roaring 87,000.

question: "Three Lions" was released for the European Championship held in England.
explainer: Thirty years of hurt — and a chorus the nation still won't stop singing.

question: "The Full Monty", about Sheffield steelworkers turned strippers, was released.
explainer: Redundancy, dignity, and a surprising amount of nudity.

question: Queen Elizabeth II died at Balmoral after 70 years on the throne.
explainer: The longest reign in British history came quietly to a close.

question: England brought in the 5p charge for single-use carrier bags.
explainer: And suddenly everyone owned nineteen "bags for life".

question: The Duke of Wellington defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo.
explainer: "A damn near-run thing," said the Duke. ABBA agreed, much later.

question: Brian Clough's Nottingham Forest won the European Cup for the first time.
explainer: Promoted, champions, then kings of Europe — twice. Utterly absurd.

question: The Beatles released their debut single, "Love Me Do".
explainer: Number seventeen. The follow-ups picked up a touch.

question: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the summit of Everest on a British expedition.
explainer: The news reached London the morning of the Coronation. Show-offs.

question: England regained the Ashes in the epic home series against Australia.
explainer: Flintoff, Pietersen and a summer nobody who watched has forgotten.

question: The Who released "My Generation".
explainer: Hoping to die before they got old. All now comfortably retired.

question: "Dad's Army" first marched onto BBC television.
explainer: Stupid boy. Nine series and national-treasure status followed.

question: A.A. Milne's "Winnie-the-Pooh" was first published.
explainer: A bear of very little brain, and quite enormous staying power.

question: The DeLorean DMC-12 sports car was first produced, in Northern Ireland.
explainer: Stainless steel, gullwing doors, and a rather good film role to come.

question: "The Italian Job", with its Mini getaway, opened in cinemas.
explainer: You were only supposed to blow the bloody doors off.

question: Nelson defeated the French and Spanish fleets at the Battle of Trafalgar.
explainer: The signal flew, the fleet won, and Nelson didn't come home.

question: David Attenborough's landmark series "Life on Earth" first aired on the BBC.
explainer: Thirteen episodes that made the whole planet the star.

question: The Forth Bridge, the great red railway cantilever, opened over the Firth of Forth.
explainer: Painting it became the byword for a job that's never quite done.

question: The Sony Walkman personal cassette player went on sale.
explainer: Suddenly your music came with you, and nobody else could hear it.

question: The murder-mystery board game Cluedo was launched by Waddingtons of Leeds.
explainer: Dreamed up in wartime Britain to pass the hours indoors. It caught on.

question: The Wombles first appeared on children's television, tidying Wimbledon Common.
explainer: Litter-picking furry creatures, with a suspiciously funky pop career.

question: "Four Weddings and a Funeral" made Hugh Grant a household name.
explainer: Bumbling, charming, and box-office gold on a shoestring budget.

question: Joseph Bazalgette began building London's great sewer network after the Great Stink.
explainer: The smell finally shamed Parliament into cleaning up the Thames.

question: Ken Loach's film "Kes", about a Barnsley boy and his kestrel, was released.
explainer: A two-fingered salute and one of the great British heartbreakers.

question: Billy Butlin opened his first holiday camp, at Skegness.
explainer: Redcoats, knobbly-knees contests and rain-or-shine jollity for the masses.

question: The Lovell Telescope at Jodrell Bank began scanning the skies over Cheshire.
explainer: Finished just in time to track Sputnik, which was terribly convenient.

question: Michael Caine's gangland thriller "Get Carter" was filmed around Newcastle.
explainer: A pint of bitter in a thin glass, and Tyneside at its bleakest.

question: "Auf Wiedersehen, Pet", about Geordie brickies working in Germany, first aired.
explainer: Seven blokes, one hut, and a great deal of homesickness.

question: The very first FA Cup final was played, at the Kennington Oval.
explainer: Wanderers lifted it. The old pot's been chased ever since.

question: The Flying Scotsman made the first non-stop run from London to Edinburgh.
explainer: Ten hours flat, with a corridor tender so the crew could swap mid-gallop.

question: Rod Stewart topped the charts with "Maggie May".
explainer: Every picture tells a story — this one stayed number one for weeks.

question: "Kind Hearts and Coronets", the Ealing black comedy, reached cinemas.
explainer: Alec Guinness played all eight doomed members of one unlucky family.

question: Manchester United became the first English club to win the European Cup.
explainer: Ten years in the making, and a famous night under the Wembley lights.

question: Geoff Hurst scored a hat-trick as England won the football World Cup final at Wembley.
explainer: It is now. The only hat-trick in a World Cup final, to this day.

question: The Beatles released "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band".
explainer: The album that turned pop into art — moustaches very much included.

question: Isaac Newton published his "Principia", setting out gravity and the laws of motion.
explainer: Some maths, one apple (allegedly), and the universe explained.

question: "Match of the Day" was first broadcast on the BBC.
explainer: Liverpool v Arsenal, and a theme tune every fan can still hum.

question: "Dr. No", the very first James Bond film, reached cinemas.
explainer: Sean Connery, a Walther PPK, and sixty-odd years of sequels.

question: The coronation of Queen Elizabeth II took place at Westminster Abbey.
explainer: The first coronation shown live on TV — the nation rushed out to buy sets.

question: Kate Bush's "Wuthering Heights" reached number one.
explainer: The first UK number one written and performed by a woman.

question: Frank Whittle ran the first British jet engine on a test bench.
explainer: Everyone told him it would never work. It rather did.

question: Celtic became the first British club to win the European Cup, in Lisbon.
explainer: Every player born within thirty miles of the ground. Never repeated.

question: Channel 4 launched, opening with the quiz show "Countdown".
explainer: A new channel, and a clock that's been ticking ever since.

question: "Chariots of Fire", about two British Olympic sprinters, was released.
explainer: Running on the sand to a synth theme that defined the decade.

question: Charles Darwin published "On the Origin of Species".
explainer: It sold out the first day. The arguments took a little longer.

question: The Stone Roses released their self-titled debut album.
explainer: Baggy trousers, jangly guitars, and a mountain of swagger.

question: Sir Steve Redgrave won a fifth consecutive Olympic rowing gold, in Sydney.
explainer: Five Games, five golds. Then a very well-earned retirement.

question: Brunel's SS Great Britain, the first iron-hulled screw-propelled liner, was launched.
explainer: Iron hull, screw propeller, and the shape of every ship to follow.

question: "Blackadder" first aired on the BBC.
explainer: Four series, four centuries, and one increasingly cunning Baldrick.

question: Robbie Williams released "Angels".
explainer: The song that turned a boyband runaway into a stadium act.

question: The famous "surgeon's photograph" of the Loch Ness Monster was published.
explainer: A grainy neck, a gripped nation, and — much later — a confessed hoax.

question: Virginia Wade won the Wimbledon ladies' singles title.
explainer: In Jubilee year, with the Queen watching. Impeccable timing.

question: "Lawrence of Arabia" swept into cinemas.
explainer: Four hours, endless desert, and one of the great film scores.

question: Christopher Cockerell's hovercraft crossed the English Channel.
explainer: It floated on a cushion of air, and was gloriously loud.

question: The Clash released their double album "London Calling".
explainer: Punk grew up — and smashed a bass on the cover doing it.

question: "Porridge", the prison sitcom starring Ronnie Barker, first aired.
explainer: Norman Stanley Fletcher: a lag, a wit, and a national treasure.

question: The world's first public steam railway, the Stockton & Darlington, opened.
explainer: Locomotion No. 1 up front, and the railway age away from the platform.

question: Dame Kelly Holmes won both 800m and 1500m gold at the Athens Olympics.
explainer: Two golds, and a look of pure disbelief each time she crossed the line.

question: Duran Duran released their album "Rio".
explainer: Yachts, New Romantics, and MTV's favourite Brummies.

question: "A Hard Day's Night", the Beatles' first film, was released.
explainer: A day in the life of Beatlemania, played beautifully for laughs.

question: Dolly the Sheep, the first cloned mammal, was born at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh.
explainer: Named after Dolly Parton, for reasons best not dwelt upon.

question: "The Good Life" first aired, with the Goods going self-sufficient in Surbiton.
explainer: Pigs, plotting the neighbours, and suburban self-sufficiency.

question: Nigel Mansell won the Formula One World Championship.
explainer: A moustache, a raised finger, and Britain's most popular driver.

question: The Jam reached number one with "Going Underground".
explainer: Woking's finest, entering right at the top of the charts.

question: Greenwich was adopted as the world's Prime Meridian.
explainer: Longitude zero — and the world set its clocks by us.

question: Bill Forsyth's Scottish teen comedy "Gregory's Girl" was released.
explainer: Football, first love, and Cumbernauld in the sunshine.

question: Arsenal went through an entire league season unbeaten.
explainer: Thirty-eight games, not a single defeat. Still the only ones to do it.

question: Eurythmics released "Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)".
explainer: Annie Lennox, a flame-orange crop, and a synth line for the ages.

question: "Grandstand", the BBC's Saturday sports institution, was first broadcast.
explainer: Results clattering in, and a nation checking its pools coupon.

question: The de Havilland Comet, the world's first jet airliner, entered passenger service.
explainer: Britain led the jet age — for a little while, at least.

question: Culture Club topped the charts with "Karma Chameleon".
explainer: Boy George, a hat, and the biggest-selling UK single of its year.

question: Frankie Dettori rode all seven winners on a single card at Ascot.
explainer: The bookies wept. The accumulator odds were over 25,000 to one.

question: "Trainspotting", from Irvine Welsh's Edinburgh novel, hit cinemas.
explainer: Choose a soundtrack absolutely everyone owned.

question: The world's first traffic lights were installed outside the Houses of Parliament.
explainer: Gas-powered — and they promptly exploded. Back to the drawing board.

question: T. Rex and Marc Bolan launched glam rock with "Get It On".
explainer: Platform boots optional, but very much encouraged.

question: Linford Christie won Olympic 100m gold in Barcelona.
explainer: Britain's fastest man, away first and never caught.

question: "Yes Minister" first aired, skewering the ways of Whitehall.
explainer: Jim Hacker, Sir Humphrey, and the civil service running rings.

question: Elizabeth II marked her Silver Jubilee — 25 years on the throne.
explainer: Street parties, bunting, and beacons the length of the land.

question: The Verve released "Bitter Sweet Symphony".
explainer: A swaggering string loop — and a famously expensive lawsuit.

question: "A Fish Called Wanda" paired John Cleese with Jamie Lee Curtis and Kevin Kline.
explainer: Heists, double-crosses, and a very unlucky aquarium.

question: Stephen Hawking published "A Brief History of Time".
explainer: The best-selling book that almost nobody actually finished.

question: Damon Hill won the Formula One World Championship.
explainer: Following his father Graham — the only son of a champion to manage it.

question: "Are You Being Served?" opened the doors of Grace Brothers department store.
explainer: Mr Humphries, Mrs Slocombe, and endless double meanings.

question: Greenwich Mean Time was adopted as Britain's single legal standard of time.
explainer: The railways needed everyone on the same clock. Sensible, really.

question: Take That returned to number one with "Back for Good".
explainer: Rain, white shirts, and the ballad that defined the band.

question: "Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels" announced Guy Ritchie to cinema.
explainer: Card games gone wrong, and a great deal of very sharp dialogue.

question: Barry Sheene won motorcycling's 500cc World Championship.
explainer: A grin, a plaster cast or two, and Britain's biking hero.

question: "'Allo 'Allo!" first aired, its farce set in a French café.
explainer: I shall say this only once — it ran for nine cheerful series.

question: Madness reached number one with "House of Fun".
explainer: The Nutty Boys' only chart-topper, and a rite-of-passage tale.

question: EMI's first CT scanner, a British invention, scanned its first patient.
explainer: Funded, improbably, by the profits from the Beatles' record label.

question: Sir Chris Hoy won three cycling golds at the Beijing Olympics.
explainer: Three golds in a week, and a velodrome later named after him.

question: "Billy Elliot" danced into cinemas.
explainer: A County Durham lad, ballet shoes, and not a dry eye in the house.

question: The first University Boat Race between Oxford and Cambridge was rowed.
explainer: Oxford took the first one. They've been squabbling over the water since.

question: Cliff Richard and the Shadows topped the charts with "Living Doll".
explainer: Britain's answer to Elvis — with considerably better longevity.

question: "The Two Ronnies" first appeared on the BBC.
explainer: Fork handles, and it's goodnight from him.

question: Wimbledon's "Crazy Gang" beat mighty Liverpool to win the FA Cup.
explainer: The Culture Club beaten by the Crazy Gang, as the man said.

question: The Kinks released "Waterloo Sunset".
explainer: A dirty old river, two lovers, and pure paradise.

question: "Monty Python and the Holy Grail" clip-clopped into cinemas.
explainer: Coconuts for horses, and a distinctly aggressive rabbit.

question: Michael Faraday demonstrated electromagnetic induction at the Royal Institution.
explainer: The principle behind every electric generator you've ever used.

question: Jenson Button won the Formula One World Championship.
explainer: A long apprenticeship, one brilliant car, and a title at last.

question: "Rainbow", with Zippy, George and Bungle, first appeared on ITV.
explainer: Zippy talked far, far too much. Bungle wore no trousers.

question: Madame Tussaud opened her permanent waxwork exhibition on Baker Street.
explainer: Wax kings, wax villains, and a very long queue ever since.

question: Arctic Monkeys released the fastest-selling debut album in British chart history.
explainer: Sheffield lads, MySpace hype, and a genuinely brilliant record.

question: "Shaun of the Dead" invented the zombie romantic comedy.
explainer: A cricket bat, a red tie, and a pint at the Winchester.

question: Denise Lewis won Olympic heptathlon gold in Sydney.
explainer: Seven events, two days, and one very hard-won gold medal.

question: Franz Ferdinand released "Take Me Out".
explainer: Glasgow art-rock, and a riff that changes gear halfway through.

question: "Bagpuss" was first shown on children's television.
explainer: Only thirteen episodes ever made, and adored beyond all reason.

question: The Spitfire made its maiden flight from Eastleigh aerodrome.
explainer: R.J. Mitchell's curved wing, and a silhouette everyone knows.

question: Daley Thompson retained his Olympic decathlon title in Los Angeles.
explainer: Ten events, two Games running, and a cheeky whistle on the podium.

question: Tears for Fears released "Everybody Wants to Rule the World".
explainer: Bath's finest, and a chorus that still turns up everywhere.

question: Brunel's Clifton Suspension Bridge opened over the Avon Gorge at Bristol.
explainer: Finished after his death, as a monument to the man in the tall hat.

question: "Withnail and I" staggered into cinemas.
explainer: Two out-of-work actors, one Cumbrian cottage, and the finest tea scene in film.

question: "The Office", Ricky Gervais's mockumentary, first aired on the BBC.
explainer: Slough, a cringing boss, and the template for a genre.

question: The first London Marathon was run through the capital's streets.
explainer: The two leaders crossed the line holding hands. Very British.

question: Dexys Midnight Runners hit number one with "Come On Eileen".
explainer: Dungarees, fiddles, and the best-selling single of the year.

question: "Chicken Run", Aardman's plasticine great escape, reached cinemas.
explainer: Poultry, a pie machine, and a daring dash for freedom.

question: John Logie Baird demonstrated the first working television.
explainer: A ventriloquist's dummy, flickering, in a Soho attic.

question: Manchester City won the league title with a goal deep in stoppage time.
explainer: 93 minutes and 20 seconds — the most dramatic finish the league has seen.

question: Girls Aloud were formed on the TV talent show "Popstars: The Rivals".
explainer: The most successful reality-TV band Britain has produced, no contest.

question: "Postman Pat" and his black-and-white cat first made their rounds.
explainer: Greendale, a little red van, and letters that always got through.

question: "Bridget Jones's Diary" opened, with Renée Zellweger as the Borough singleton.
explainer: Chardonnay, blue soup, and not one but two suitors.

question: England's cricketers won the ICC Women's World Cup final at a packed Lord's.
explainer: A sell-out crowd, a nail-biting finish, and a new era for the women's game.

question: The London Eye observation wheel opened to the public on the South Bank.
explainer: Meant to be temporary. Now as much London as the river beneath it.

question: J.K. Rowling's "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" was first published.
explainer: A first print run of just 500 copies. It did all right in the end.

question: Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine, against smallpox.
explainer: He used cowpox — 'vaccine' comes from the Latin for cow.

question: Dennis Taylor beat Steve Davis on the final black in the World Snooker final.
explainer: Past midnight, 18.5 million watched him wag his finger in delight.

question: David Bowie released "Space Oddity".
explainer: Ground Control to Major Tom, timed neatly for the Moon-landing summer.

question: "The Sweeney", the hard-boiled cop show, first aired.
explainer: Shut it. Ford Cortinas, villains, and Regan and Carter.

question: Tower Bridge opened across the River Thames.
explainer: Not London Bridge — the one everyone photographs by mistake.

question: Alcock and Brown made the first non-stop transatlantic flight, landing in Ireland.
explainer: Sixteen hours in an open cockpit, ending nose-down in an Irish bog.

question: The Police released "Every Breath You Take".
explainer: A song about obsession the whole world decided to play at weddings.

question: "The Ladykillers", the Ealing comedy, was released.
explainer: Alec Guinness, a sweet old landlady, and a robbery that unravels beautifully.

question: Jim Laker took 19 wickets in a single Test match against Australia.
explainer: Nineteen out of a possible twenty. Surely never to be beaten.

question: The Royal Society, the world's oldest national scientific academy, was founded.
explainer: Nullius in verba — take nobody's word for it. Quite right too.

question: Procol Harum released "A Whiter Shade of Pale".
explainer: A Bach-ish organ, cryptic words, and the sound of the Summer of Love.

question: "Steptoe and Son", the rag-and-bone-man sitcom, first aired.
explainer: Harold and his father Albert — 'you dirty old man'.

question: Stanley Matthews finally won an FA Cup winner's medal in the 'Matthews Final'.
explainer: At 38, the Wizard of the Dribble dragged Blackpool back from 3–1 down.

question: Helen Sharman became the first Briton in space, visiting the Mir station.
explainer: A chemist from Sheffield, chosen after answering an advert on the radio.

question: 10cc released "I'm Not in Love".
explainer: That whispering wall of voices — 'big boys don't cry'.

question: "Oliver!", the musical film of Dickens's novel, reached cinemas.
explainer: Please, sir, I want some more — and a clutch of Oscars followed.

question: Thomas Telford's Menai Suspension Bridge opened to the island of Anglesey.
explainer: The longest span in the world at the time, slung across the strait.

question: The first McDonald's in the UK opened, in Woolwich, south-east London.
explainer: A Big Mac in Woolwich. Britain's high streets would never be quite the same.

question: Rupert Murdoch bought The Sun newspaper.
explainer: He relaunched it as a tabloid within weeks. The rest is very loud history.

question: Paul McCartney and Wings went to number one with "Mull of Kintyre".
explainer: Bagpipes, a Scottish peninsula, and the first UK single to sell two million copies.

question: Castlemaine XXXX lager was first introduced to the UK.
explainer: Brewed here under licence, and sold on the idea that Australians wouldn't give a XXXX for anything else.

question: Back to the Future was released in British cinemas.
explainer: Marty McFly, a DeLorean, and 1.21 gigawatts. Great Scott!

question: Michael Owen scored a wonder goal against Argentina at the World Cup.
explainer: An eighteen-year-old, half the length of the pitch, and a nation on its feet.

question: "Bend It Like Beckham" scored a surprise box-office hit.
explainer: Football, family and freedom, in a Hounslow back garden.

question: Amazon.co.uk opened for business, selling only books.
explainer: Just books to begin with. Then, eventually, absolutely everything.

question: Wet Wet Wet's "Love Is All Around" spent 15 weeks at number one.
explainer: From Four Weddings and a Funeral. They deleted it themselves to make it stop.

question: Tesco launched its Clubcard loyalty scheme.
explainer: Points for your shopping, and a lot of data for Tesco. Everybody won. Sort of.

question: Michael Jackson released the album "Thriller".
explainer: The best-selling album of all time, and a zombie dance routine.

question: Emma Raducanu won the US Open as a qualifier, without dropping a set.
explainer: Eighteen years old, ranked outside the top 100, and a fairy tale in New York.

question: Joe Dolce's "Shaddap You Face" kept Ultravox's "Vienna" off number one.
explainer: Midge Ure has never quite got over it. Understandably.

question: Paula Radcliffe set a women's marathon world record that stood for 16 years.
explainer: London, two hours fifteen, and miles clear of everyone else.

question: The Nescafé Gold Blend couple began their will-they-won't-they adverts.
explainer: A soap opera in forty-second chunks, all over a jar of coffee.

question: Lilt, with its 'totally tropical taste', was launched.
explainer: Pineapple and grapefruit in a can, all the way from... Coca-Cola.

question: Gerry and the Pacemakers took "You'll Never Walk Alone" to number one.
explainer: A Merseybeat cover that became football's most stirring anthem.

question: Sky Television launched, beaming four channels to dishes across Britain.
explainer: Squarials, Sky One, and grumbling about dishes on the front of houses.

question: "Blind Date" first aired, with Cilla Black.
explainer: 'A lorra lorra laughs.' And quite a few awkward holidays.

question: Anita Roddick opened the first Body Shop, in Brighton.
explainer: Refillable bottles and no animal testing, long before anyone else bothered.

question: "Educating Rita", with Michael Caine and Julie Walters, was released.
explainer: A weary tutor, a Liverpudlian hairdresser, and Willy Russell's wit.

question: Viz comic was first published, in Newcastle.
explainer: Roger Mellie, the Fat Slags and Sid the Sexist. Never knowingly tasteful.

question: "Top of the Pops" was first broadcast.
explainer: Chart hits, dodgy miming, and a Thursday-night ritual for decades.

question: The Sony PlayStation went on sale in the UK.
explainer: Wipeout, Tomb Raider, and the console that made gaming cool for grown-ups.

question: "Peep Show" first aired on Channel 4.
explainer: Mark and Jeremy, filmed from the inside of their heads.

question: Red Bull went on sale in the UK.
explainer: It gives you wings, apparently. Also, a slight twitch.

question: Bonnie Tyler reached number one with "Total Eclipse of the Heart".
explainer: Turn around, bright eyes. Welsh gravel and Wagnerian drama.

question: "Have I Got News For You" first aired.
explainer: Satire with Ian Hislop and Paul Merton. Plus a tub of lard, once.

question: BBC iPlayer launched.
explainer: No more setting the video. Catch-up TV went mainstream.

question: New Order released "Blue Monday", the best-selling 12-inch single ever.
explainer: The elaborate sleeve cost so much they lost money on every copy sold.

question: "Bullseye" first aired, with Jim Bowen.
explainer: 'Look at what you could have won.' Usually a speedboat.

question: The Premier League kicked off its very first season.
explainer: Sky's money, Monday Night Football, and the game changed forever.

question: The Raleigh Chopper bike was launched in Britain.
explainer: High-rise handlebars, a gearstick between your legs. Health and safety looked away.

question: Guinness's 'Surfer' advert, with its galloping white horses, first aired.
explainer: Tick follows tock follows tick. Regularly voted the best advert ever made.

question: "Ghostbusters" was released.
explainer: Who you gonna call? Everybody knew the answer.

question: "Thunderbirds", Gerry Anderson's Supermarionation series, launched.
explainer: F.A.B. Puppets, strings, exploding models, and International Rescue.

question: "The Young Ones", the anarchic student sitcom, first aired.
explainer: Rick, Vyvyan, Neil and Mike, and the birth of alternative comedy.

question: Spotify launched in the UK.
explainer: All the music in the world, and the slow death of the CD rack.

question: "Top Gun" was released.
explainer: Aviators, volleyball, and a need for speed.

question: "Neighbours" was first shown on BBC One.
explainer: Ramsay Street at lunchtime, and again at teatime for those who missed it.

question: easyJet's first flight took off, from Luton to Glasgow.
explainer: Tickets 'as cheap as a pair of jeans'. Orange everything.

question: Blackburn Rovers, bankrolled by Jack Walker, won the Premier League.
explainer: Shearer, Sutton and small-town Lancashire, briefly on top of England.

question: Rupert Murdoch bought The Times.
explainer: The Thunderer joined The Sun in the same stable. Not everyone was thrilled.

question: "Last of the Summer Wine", the world's longest-running sitcom, first aired.
explainer: Three old Yorkshiremen, a tin bath, and a very steep hill.

question: lastminute.com was founded by Martha Lane Fox and Brent Hoberman.
explainer: The poster child of the dotcom boom, selling holidays and theatre tickets.

question: Del Boy fell through the bar in "Only Fools and Horses".
explainer: A lean on the bar, a perfectly timed fall. Possibly the most repeated moment in British comedy.

question: The iPhone went on sale in the UK, exclusively on O2.
explainer: Touchscreens, apps, and nobody looking up from their phone ever again.

question: Oasis released "Wonderwall".
explainer: Every busker's favourite. Still played at every party you've ever been to.

question: "Dallas" viewers finally found out who shot J.R.
explainer: It was Kristin. The whole country stayed in to find out.

question: Tate Modern opened in the old Bankside power station on the Thames.
explainer: A vast turbine hall, and modern art for the millions.

question: Coca-Cola's 'Holidays are coming' lorries first appeared on British TV.
explainer: The unofficial start of Christmas for a whole generation.

question: "Notting Hill", the Richard Curtis romantic comedy, was released.
explainer: A travel bookshop, a film star, and 'just a girl, standing in front of a boy'.

question: Rage Against the Machine beat The X Factor to the Christmas number one.
explainer: A Facebook campaign against Simon Cowell, and it actually worked.

question: Starbucks arrived in Britain by buying the Seattle Coffee Company.
explainer: Lattes to go, and your name spelt wrong on the cup, from then on.

question: André Previn joined Morecambe and Wise, playing 'all the right notes'.
explainer: 'But not necessarily in the right order.' Christmas TV gold.

question: Ed Sheeran released "Shape of You".
explainer: Streamed into the billions. And played in every gym in the land.

question: Cadbury's Wispa went on sale across the whole country.
explainer: All those bubbles. Axed, then brought back by a Facebook campaign.

question: "Love Actually" was released.
explainer: Billy Mack, Hugh Grant's dancing PM, and those cue cards.

question: The new Wembley Stadium opened, with its giant arch.
explainer: Years late, wildly over budget, and well worth the wait. Mostly.

question: The Guinness Book of Records was first published.
explainer: Born from a pub argument about Europe's fastest game bird.

question: "Jaws" was released, and people were scared to go back in the water.
explainer: Da dum. Da dum. The first summer blockbuster.

question: Monster Munch crisps were launched.
explainer: Originally called The Prime Monster. Pickled onion was, and is, the correct flavour.

question: Kim Wilde released "Kids in America".
explainer: New Wave pop out of Hertfordshire, conquering the airwaves.

question: The Animals released "The House of the Rising Sun".
explainer: A Newcastle band, an old American folk tune, and a haunting organ.

question: The 'You know when you've been Tango'd' advert first aired.
explainer: An orange man slapping people. Pulled after playground copycats.

question: Daniel Craig made his James Bond debut in "Casino Royale".
explainer: Blond Bond, those blue trunks, and some very sceptical critics proved wrong.

question: Apple launched the very first iPod.
explainer: A thousand songs in your pocket, and white earphones everywhere.

question: The National Lottery held its very first draw.
explainer: Mystic Meg, a giant pointing finger, and 'It could be you'.

question: Ceefax, the BBC's teletext service, was launched.
explainer: Page 302 for the football scores, while the jazz played.

question: Netflix launched its streaming service in the UK.
explainer: Binge-watching was about to become a national pastime.

question: "Grange Hill", the gritty comprehensive-school drama, first rang its bell.
explainer: School life with all the warts, and sausages on forks, left in.

question: The first Glastonbury Festival took place, at Worthy Farm.
explainer: Tickets cost £1, and that included free milk from the farm.

question: "The Wicker Man", the great British folk-horror, was released.
explainer: A remote Scottish isle, pagan rites, and a genuinely alarming ending.

question: "The Royle Family" first aired.
explainer: A family, a sofa, a telly. 'My arse!'

question: Cadbury's drumming gorilla advert first aired.
explainer: Phil Collins, 'In the Air Tonight', and a gorilla who really, really meant it.

question: ABBA won Eurovision with "Waterloo", in Brighton.
explainer: Glitter, platform boots, and four Swedes on the way to world domination.

question: "Absolutely Fabulous" first aired, with Edina and Patsy behaving very badly.
explainer: Sweetie darling, endless Bolly, and the funniest excess on television.

question: Marathon bars were renamed Snickers in the UK.
explainer: Same peanuts, new name, and decades of people still calling it a Marathon.

question: Dr. Martens made their first 1460 boot, in Northamptonshire.
explainer: Named after its birthday: the first of April. From postmen to punks.

question: "Gavin & Stacey" first aired.
explainer: Essex meets Barry Island. 'Oh, what's occurring?'

question: Liverpool came from 3-0 down to win the Champions League in Istanbul.
explainer: Half-time at 3-0, and somehow champions by the end of the night.

question: Dizzee Rascal's "Boy in da Corner" won the Mercury Prize.
explainer: East London grime, aged nineteen, and a genuine game-changer.

question: Ridley Scott's Hovis 'boy on the bike' advert first aired.
explainer: Dvorak, a cobbled hill in Shaftesbury, and a loaf in a basket.

question: "Big Brother" first aired in the UK.
explainer: Nasty Nick, a house full of cameras, and reality TV took over.

question: Pirate station Radio Caroline first broadcast from a ship in the North Sea.
explainer: Pop music the BBC wouldn't play, from international waters.

question: The first Penguin paperbacks went on sale for sixpence each.
explainer: Proper books at cigarette prices. Reading, for absolutely everyone.

question: The Range Rover was launched.
explainer: A luxury car that could go up a muddy hill. Chelsea's farmers rejoiced.

question: Ford launched the Cortina.
explainer: Britain's best-selling car for years. The sales rep's chariot.

question: Comic Relief held its very first Red Nose Day.
explainer: Red noses on cars, people, and occasionally on lorries.

question: The Independent newspaper was launched.
explainer: 'It is. Are you?' A brand new broadsheet with no proprietor.

question: TV-am launched breakfast television on ITV, with its 'Famous Five' presenters.
explainer: Then Roland Rat came along and saved the day.

question: Roxy Music released their glam debut single "Virginia Plain".
explainer: Bryan Ferry, feathers, and pure art-school cool.

question: British Leyland launched the Austin Allegro.
explainer: The square steering wheel was called the 'Quartic'. It did not catch on.

question: Channel 5 launched, opening with the Spice Girls.
explainer: First, millions of people had to retune their video recorders.

question: The world's first text message was sent, over the Vodafone network.
explainer: It said 'Merry Christmas'. Sent from a computer, as phones couldn't type yet.

question: The Pogues and Kirsty MacColl released "Fairytale of New York".
explainer: The best Christmas song never to reach number one.

question: BBC Radio 1 launched, with Tony Blackburn at the microphone.
explainer: The first record played was 'Flowers in the Rain' by The Move.

question: Aldi opened its first UK store, in Birmingham.
explainer: Stechford, of all places. Middle aisle madness had arrived.

question: Mr Blobby was the Christmas number one.
explainer: A big pink spotty blob beat Take That. Britain, explain yourself.

question: Soft Cell's "Tainted Love" topped the UK charts.
explainer: A Northern Soul cover reborn as the sound of synth-pop.

question: "Grease" was released.
explainer: Danny, Sandy, and a soundtrack that still fills every wedding dance floor.

question: Nokia launched the 3310 mobile phone.
explainer: Indestructible, a battery that lasted a week, and Snake II.

question: Loaded, the original 'lads' mag', was launched.
explainer: 'For men who should know better.' And mostly didn't.

question: Ernie Wise made the UK's first public mobile phone call.
explainer: On a phone the size of a house brick, on New Year's Day.

question: "Jurassic Park" was released.
explainer: Dinosaurs brought to life, and a glass of water that wobbled.

question: Anthony Joshua beat Wladimir Klitschko in front of 90,000 at Wembley.
explainer: A knockdown, a comeback, and one of the great heavyweight nights.

question: Domino's delivered its first pizza in the UK, from a shop in Luton.
explainer: A pizza at your door in thirty minutes was pure science fiction until then.

question: "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial" was released.
explainer: E.T. phone home. And a bike flying across the moon.

question: The free Metro newspaper was launched on the London Underground.
explainer: Read on the Tube, left on the seat, read by the next person.

question: The PG Tips chimps starred in their first TV advert.
explainer: Chimps having a tea party. It ran, in various forms, for decades.

question: Frank Bruno finally became world heavyweight champion, at Wembley.
explainer: 'Know what I mean, Harry?' Fourth time lucky.

question: Bryan Adams spent 16 weeks at number one with "(Everything I Do) I Do It for You".
explainer: Robin Hood's theme tune, all summer long. Everyone was quite sick of it.

question: "Inspector Morse" first aired, with John Thaw as the Oxford detective.
explainer: Crosswords, real ale, a maroon Jaguar and a great deal of Wagner.

question: Baileys Irish Cream went on sale.
explainer: Whiskey and cream in one bottle. Christmas drinks cabinets everywhere rejoiced.

question: Travis released the album "The Man Who".
explainer: 'Why Does It Always Rain on Me?' Post-Britpop melancholy, done beautifully.

question: The Sun ran its famous 'Gotcha' headline during the Falklands War.
explainer: Probably the most infamous front page in Fleet Street history.

question: Pizza Hut opened its first UK restaurant, in Islington.
explainer: Red roofs, the salad bar tower challenge, and birthday treats for a generation.

question: "Multi-Coloured Swap Shop", with Noel Edmonds, first aired.
explainer: Swapping your Action Man for a skateboard, live on BBC One.

question: Pot Noodle first went on sale.
explainer: Just add boiling water. And, for many, a small amount of shame.

question: Phil Collins released "In the Air Tonight".
explainer: That drum fill. You know the one. Everybody air-drums it.

question: Wall's launched Viennetta.
explainer: Ice cream with crunchy chocolate layers. The height of dinner-party sophistication.

question: Freeview launched, rising from the ashes of ITV Digital.
explainer: Digital telly with no subscription. And no knitted monkey.

question: Henry Cooper floored Muhammad Ali with a left hook known as 'Enry's 'Ammer.
explainer: Down went the great man, before a split glove bought him time to recover.

question: Rowntree's launched the Yorkie bar, aimed squarely at lorry drivers.
explainer: Chunky, manly, and later, rather unwisely, 'not for girls'.

question: "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" first aired, with Chris Tarrant.
explainer: Phone a friend, ask the audience, and 'is that your final answer?'

question: Chelsea won the Champions League for the first time, in Munich.
explainer: Didier Drogba, a header, and the winning penalty.

question: Private Eye published its first issue.
explainer: Lord Gnome's organ, and a great many lawsuits.

question: The world's first cash machine opened, outside Barclays in Enfield.
explainer: Reg Varney, of On the Buses, made the first withdrawal. Using a paper voucher.

question: Wallace and Gromit's "The Wrong Trousers" was first shown.
explainer: Techno trousers, a sinister penguin, and that train-track chase.

question: The Manchester Guardian dropped 'Manchester' from its name.
explainer: Plain old The Guardian from then on. The move to London came later.

question: Nick Kamen stripped to his boxers in the Levi's launderette advert.
explainer: Sales of 501s went through the roof. So did sales of boxer shorts.

question: "Doctor Who" returned to TV, with Christopher Eccleston as the Doctor.
explainer: Sixteen years off air, then straight back to Saturday-night glory.

question: The Austin Metro was launched, 'a British car to beat the world'.
explainer: Lady Diana drove one. Sales, briefly, were very good indeed.

question: James Hunt won the Formula One World Championship.
explainer: A playboy, a rival named Lauda, and a title settled in the Japanese rain.

question: "The X Factor" first aired.
explainer: Simon Cowell, sob stories, and a Christmas number one machine.

question: "Father Ted" first aired on Channel 4.
explainer: Craggy Island, Mrs Doyle, and 'down with this sort of thing'.

question: Barclaycard, Britain's first credit card, was launched.
explainer: Plastic money arrived, and spending what you didn't have became very easy indeed.

question: Manic Street Preachers released "A Design for Life".
explainer: Libraries gave us power, and Welsh rock one of its finest anthems.

question: KFC opened its first UK branch, in Preston.
explainer: The Colonel's secret recipe made its British debut in Lancashire.

question: Mike Oldfield's "Tubular Bells" became the very first Virgin Records release.
explainer: It started Richard Branson's empire. Then it scored The Exorcist.

question: "Spitting Image", the satirical puppet show, first appeared.
explainer: Grotesque latex politicians, and absolutely nobody spared.

question: The Shadows topped the charts with the instrumental "Apache".
explainer: Hank Marvin's twangy guitar, and a thousand bedroom guitarists born.

question: "Raiders of the Lost Ark" was released.
explainer: Indiana Jones, a giant boulder, and snakes. Why did it have to be snakes?

question: Dyson launched its first bagless vacuum cleaner, the DC01.
explainer: After more than 5,000 prototypes in a shed. Persistence, thy name is James.

question: "Gladiators" first aired on ITV.
explainer: Wolf, Jet, Lightning, and the dreaded Eliminator.

question: IKEA opened its first UK store, in Warrington.
explainer: Flat-pack furniture, meatballs, and the very first arguments over missing screws.

question: Suede released their self-titled debut album.
explainer: The band that lit the fuse for Britpop, all glamour and gloom.

question: "Star Wars" opened in British cinemas.
explainer: A long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away. Queues round the block.

question: Smash Hits magazine was first published.
explainer: Song lyrics, posters, and 'Black Type' for every pop fan.

question: Tamagotchi virtual pets arrived in Britain.
explainer: Feed it, clean it, and watch it die during double maths. Then get it confiscated.

question: Roald Dahl's "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory" was published.
explainer: Golden tickets, a chocolate river, and one very deserving boy.

question: Compare the Market launched its meerkat adverts.
explainer: Aleksandr Orlov, 'simples', and a cuddly toy in every other house.

question: "Dirty Dancing" was released.
explainer: Nobody puts Baby in a corner. That lift, in that lake.

question: Eddie 'the Eagle' Edwards ski-jumped for Britain at the Calgary Winter Olympics.
explainer: He came last. Everybody loved him anyway.

question: "Mastermind" first aired, with Magnus Magnusson.
explainer: 'I've started, so I'll finish.' The black chair was born.

question: Virgin Atlantic made its first flight, from Gatwick to Newark.
explainer: Richard Branson's record label took to the skies. As you do.

question: Katrina and the Waves won Eurovision with "Love Shine a Light".
explainer: The UK's fifth Eurovision win. Shine a light, indeed.

question: The Smash Martians adverts first appeared, laughing at humans peeling potatoes.
explainer: 'For mash get Smash.' Tin robots, cackling, forever.

question: Sally Gunnell won Olympic 400m hurdles gold in Barcelona.
explainer: Over the barriers and away. Britain's golden girl of the track.

question: Frankie Goes to Hollywood released "Relax", which the BBC promptly banned.
explainer: The ban, naturally, sent it straight to number one.

question: Opal Fruits were renamed Starburst.
explainer: Made to make your mouth water. And your nan still calls them Opal Fruits.

question: The News of the World published its final edition.
explainer: Closed after 168 years, in the middle of the phone-hacking scandal.

question: "Skyfall", the James Bond film, was released.
explainer: Adele's theme, the Aston Martin, and Judi Dench's farewell as M.

question: Amstrad launched its CPC 464 home computer, with a built-in tape deck.
explainer: Alan Sugar's all-in-one. Plug it in and wait ten minutes for a game to load.

question: "Red Dwarf", the sci-fi sitcom, first aired.
explainer: Three million years into deep space, with a curry and a hologram.
